To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

we have developed a quantitative reverse transcriptase-polymerase chain reaction method to detect even low amounts of a small HBV mRNA species within larger ones, that this method has revealed that the mRNAs for large and small surface proteins as well as for the X protein are present in the peripheral blood mononucleated cells (PBMC) of persistently HBV infected patients but are not present in serum, and that covalently closed circular viral DNA is also found in the PBMC.
HBV replicates in PBMC from persistently infected individuals.

the possibility of an extrahepatically located replication of HBV.
the detection and quantitation of the HBV mRNAs in PBMC and serum of viremic patients.
the question of whether the HBV genome is able to replicate in mononuclear blood cell lines and whether the viral X protein is able to influence the function of these cells.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
PBMC from patients with chronic HBV infection contain viral DNA and transcripts of all three essential viral proteins, which may be the result of replication of the virus in these cells.
HBV is able to replicate in PBMC, but this has to be verified by further experiments.
HBV can replicate in PBMC, and this may be of relevance for the pathogenesis of chronic HBV infection.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
HBV is not only taken up and expressed by mononuclear cells but also replicates there.
the virus is taken up by mononuclear cells and that these may serve as a reservoir for HBV.
HBV can replicate in PBMC, that this replication may be important for persistence, and that it is regulated by the X protein.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the presence of viral mRNA species in PBMC from patients does not necessarily mean that the virus is replicating in PBMC.
